passage:
The first time I visited Kamal's clinic, I watched him with a crying child: kneeling, voice soft, making up a story about a brave elephant. Three patients later he was still smiling. I was so proud.
Then he came home at nine and I asked about his day, and he said, "Fine." I asked if he wanted dal or khichdi, and he said, "Whatever. Doesn't matter." He scrolled on his phone through dinner. For months I thought he had simply stopped caring about me.
One night I said so, gently. He put the phone down and looked stricken. "I use it all up," he said. "By the time I get home there's nothing left."
We agreed on a small thing: twenty minutes alone on the balcony when he gets in, then real time together. Some nights I, Arohi, get the soft voice now too.

qa.q: What story did Kamal make up for the crying child?
qa.a: A story about a brave elephant.

qa.q: Why did Arohi start to believe Kamal had stopped caring?
qa.a: His warmth went to patients while at home he gave one-word answers and scrolled his phone, so Arohi felt left with only the tired leftovers.

qa.q: What choice did the couple make, and why does it help?
qa.a: Twenty minutes alone on the balcony for Kamal when he gets home, so he can recharge before real time together.

qa.q: What does Kamal's line 'I use it all up' suggest about his side of it?
qa.a: He isn't cold on purpose; his patience goes into patients all day, and he is drained by the time he reaches home.

grounding: A spouse notices that their partner is patient and charming with patients but curt at home, and learns his energy is spent before he gets there.

subtype: Warm at work, cold at home [Observer]
passage:
Notes for Thursday's session with our counsellor, written by Ankita
What I've noticed about Francis over the last month:
- At work events he is warm, funny and patient. His customers at the bank adore him. Last Friday I watched him listen to an old man's complaint for twenty minutes without once checking his watch.
- At home he walks in, says "hi" and goes straight to the shower. At dinner, if I ask a question, he says, "Can we not?" On Sunday he snapped when I asked about the electricity bill.
- He doesn't seem angry with me. He seems empty.
What I did: on Monday I said, "I think you're giving all your good hours to work, and I'm getting the tired ones." He went quiet, then agreed.
What I'd like to try: one work-free evening a week, and him telling me when he's drained instead of snapping.

qa.q: How long did Francis listen to the old man's complaint?
qa.a: Twenty minutes, without once checking his watch.

qa.q: What does Ankita mean by saying Francis 'seems empty' rather than angry?
qa.a: Ankita senses that his energy is used up by the end of the day, so the curtness comes from exhaustion, not dislike.

qa.q: Which of Ankita's ideas could help most, and why?
qa.a: Asking Francis to say when he's drained instead of snapping, so Ankita knows what's happening and doesn't take it personally.

qa.q: How might Francis's customers describe him?
qa.a: As warm, funny and endlessly patient, without seeing how little is left for home.

grounding: A spouse writes down how their partner is warm and patient at work but curt and drained at home, and suggests changes before a counselling session.

subtype: Warm at work, cold at home [Observer]
passage:
Tuesday
Went to pick Manjula up from school today and watched from the gate. Forty Class 2 kids around her, and she was laughing, crouching to tie laces, praising a wobbly drawing as if it were a masterpiece. A parent stopped me: "Your wife is a saint." I agreed.
At home she dropped her bag, said, "Please don't talk to me for a bit," and lay on the sofa with her eyes shut. When I asked what she wanted for dinner, she said, "I don't care, Devika, anything." It stung. It always stings.
But I've started to see it: she isn't cold to me. She's spent. Every drop of patience goes to those forty kids. I get the empty cup.
Tomorrow I'll ask her: can we have Sunday mornings where nobody needs anything from her, and then a proper walk, just us? I miss the laughing version.
Devika

qa.q: What did the parent at the gate say to Devika?
qa.a: "Your wife is a saint."

qa.q: Why did 'I don't care, Devika, anything' sting?
qa.a: After seeing Manjula so warm with the children, the flat answer felt like getting less, even though Devika suspected she was simply drained.

qa.q: What plan does Devika make, and why might it help?
qa.a: Sunday mornings with nothing asked of Manjula, then a walk together, giving her time to refill before their time as a couple. 🤍

qa.q: What might a school day be like for Manjula?
qa.a: Constantly giving patience and warmth to forty children, which leaves her exhausted by the time she gets home.

grounding: A spouse sees their wife endlessly patient with schoolchildren but curt and drained at home, and realises her energy is spent before evening.

passage:
In Nagaur, Sachin was the agriculture officer everyone liked. On Tuesday Kashish walked past the panchayat hall and saw him with a group of farmers: crouched beside an old man, explaining the new seed scheme for the third time, laughing at a joke about goats, never once looking at his watch.
That evening he came home at eight. Kashish had kept his favourite bajra roti warm. "How was the day?" "Fine." "The seed meeting?" "Kashish, please, not now." He ate facing the TV and went to bed.
She lay awake. She had seen the patience and the laugh. They weren't gone; they just seemed used up before he reached their door.
On Sunday she said, gently, "The farmers get your best hours. Could we have one of them? Maybe Sunday morning, a walk to the lake, before your phone starts?"
Sachin was quiet, then nodded. "I didn't realise there was nothing left by the time I got home."

qa.q: What had Kashish kept warm for Sachin?
qa.a: His favourite bajra roti.

qa.q: How did Kashish feel as she lay awake that night?
qa.a: Kashish felt hurt, because she had seen Sachin's patience and laughter with the farmers, yet they seemed used up before he reached their door.

qa.q: What did Kashish's Sunday request get right?
qa.a: It named the pattern without blame and asked for one protected time, a Sunday walk before the phone starts, when Sachin still has energy.

qa.q: How might the farmers see Sachin, compared with how Kashish sees him at home?
qa.a: The farmers see a patient, cheerful officer who never checks his watch, while Kashish mostly meets a tired, curt man who comes home at eight.

grounding: Illustrates a wife who notices her husband is warm and patient with farmers but curt and drained at home, and asks for time before his energy is spent.
